# Quantitative Sensory Testing {#sec-qst}

Quantitative Sensory Testing (QST) is a set of standardized psychophysical assays that assess how pain is processed. In the Acute to Chronic Pain Signatures Study (A2CPS), we use QST to characterize each participant's pain-processing profile before surgery, on the hypothesis that these profiles help predict who goes on to develop chronic post-surgical pain.

A2CPS collects three complementary QST assays, and each one is tested at both a surgical **index site** (near where surgery will occur) and a **remote site** (a control location):

- **Pressure Pain Threshold (PPT)**: the pressure at which a steadily increasing force first becomes painful, measured with an algometer over three repetitions per site. PPT is a measure of *static* pain sensitivity. Note that **higher PPT means *less* pain sensitivity** (more pressure was needed before the participant reached pain).
- **Mechanical Temporal Summation (MTS)**: the increase in pain over a train of identical pokes delivered with a Neuropen. MTS captures *pain facilitation*, the tendency of the central nervous system to amplify repeated input. **Higher MTS means greater facilitation.**
- **Conditioned Pain Modulation (CPM)**: the change in PPT after a conditioning cold-water hand immersion. CPM captures *descending inhibition*, the "pain inhibits pain" mechanism. **Zero or positive CPM scores indicate no descending inhibition; negative scores indicate inhibition is present.**

This kit builds on the **thoracic** cohort. The NIMH Data Archive (NDA) release carries the full set of QST trials for the thoracic cohort, so all three assays can be reconstructed from the raw per-repetition ratings. The thoracic QST file already uses the HEAL Common Data Element names\ [@wandner_nih_2022], so no renaming is needed here.

For each assay, we compute a **primary** and a **secondary** outcome, and for PPT and MTS these are reported at both the index and the remote site. The definitions follow the A2CPS Manual of Procedures:

| Biomarker | Primary outcome | Secondary outcome |
|---|---|---|
| PPT | Mean PPT at the **index** site | Mean PPT at the **remote** site |
| MTS | Mean of 3 difference scores (max minus initial) | Mean of 3 wind-up ratios, (max + 1)/(initial + 1) |
| CPM | % change: (pre minus post)/pre × 100 | Difference: pre minus post |

## Starting Project

### Locate Data

The QST measure arrives from NDA as one file per cohort. We use the thoracic file. After downloading the QST structure from your NDA data package, place it under `NDA_data/` so the project looks like this:

```bash
NDA_data/
└── QST/
    └── qst_thoracic.csv
```

The code below reaches this file with `here()`, which resolves paths from the project root, so a chunk runs the same regardless of the working directory.

### Extract Data

The file is a plain CSV. We use a small set of tidyverse packages, and define two helpers for the temporal-summation formulas so the scoring chunks read cleanly.

```{r}
#| label: setup

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(here)
library(readr)
library(tidyr)

# temporal summation, per trial, from the start (initial) and end (final) pain ratings.
# the peak is the higher of the two, so a trial that ends lower than it started counts as no climb.

# how much pain climbed over the trial
ts_diff <- \(initial, final) {
  peak <- pmax(initial, final)
  peak - initial
}

# the same climb as a ratio; the +1 keeps it defined when the start rating is 0
ts_wur <- \(initial, final) {
  peak <- pmax(initial, final)
  (peak + 1) / (initial + 1)
}
```

We read the file, convert `record_id` to a number, and drop any exact duplicate rows so that a participant appears only once. We then derive the surgical cohort from `record_id`; every record here is thoracic.

```{r}
#| label: load-qst

qst <- read_csv(here("NDA_data", "QST", "qst_thoracic.csv"), skip = 1) |>
  rename(record_id = src_subject_id) |>
  mutate(record_id = as.numeric(record_id))

# guard: every record_id must parse to a number before filtering and cohort assignment
if (any(is.na(qst$record_id))) {
  stop(sum(is.na(qst$record_id)), " record_id value(s) did not parse to a number")
}

test_records <- c(10000, 15000, 20000, 25000, 40000, 50000,
                  60000, 70000, 80000, 90000, 100000, 110000, 120000)

qst <- qst |>
  distinct() |>
  filter(!record_id %in% test_records) |>
  mutate(cohort = case_when(
    record_id >= 10000 & record_id < 15000 | record_id >= 25000 ~ "TKA",
    .default = "Thoracic"
  ))
```

NDA provides the individual trial ratings rather than the summary biomarkers, so we compute them here following the A2CPS Manual of Procedures. Every mean requires all of its trials, so a missing trial yields a missing biomarker. A completion flag records which sites were tested, coded 1 for both sites, 2 for remote only, and 3 for index only. So for MTS we compute the index outcome when `TScompleted` is 1 or 3, and the remote outcome when it is 1 or 2.

For MTS, each site has three Neuropen trials. The per-trial difference is `max(final, initial) - initial`, and the wind-up ratio is `(max + 1)/(initial + 1)`. The primary outcome is the mean of the three differences, the secondary the mean of the three wind-up ratios.

```{r}
#| label: score-mts

qst <- qst |>
  mutate(
    primary_ts_index = if_else(TScompleted %in% c(1, 3),
      (ts_diff(TSindxR1initial, TSindxR1final) +
       ts_diff(TSindxR2initial, TSindxR2final) +
       ts_diff(TSindxR3initial, TSindxR3final)) / 3, NA_real_),
    secondary_ts_index = if_else(TScompleted %in% c(1, 3),
      (ts_wur(TSindxR1initial, TSindxR1final) +
       ts_wur(TSindxR2initial, TSindxR2final) +
       ts_wur(TSindxR3initial, TSindxR3final)) / 3, NA_real_),
    primary_ts_remote = if_else(TScompleted %in% c(1, 2),
      (ts_diff(TSremoteR1initial, TSremoteR1final) +
       ts_diff(TSremoteR2initial, TSremoteR2final) +
       ts_diff(TSremoteR3initial, TSremoteR3final)) / 3, NA_real_),
    secondary_ts_remote = if_else(TScompleted %in% c(1, 2),
      (ts_wur(TSremoteR1initial, TSremoteR1final) +
       ts_wur(TSremoteR2initial, TSremoteR2final) +
       ts_wur(TSremoteR3initial, TSremoteR3final)) / 3, NA_real_)
  )
```

For PPT, the primary outcome is the mean of the three index trials and the secondary the mean of the three remote trials. `PPTcompleteYN` uses the same coding as above, so the index outcome is computed when it is 1 or 3 and the remote when it is 1 or 2. CPM compares the remote PPT before conditioning (the secondary PPT) with the PPT measured during cold-water immersion; the primary outcome is the percent change and the secondary the raw difference.

```{r}
#| label: score-ppt-cpm

qst <- qst |>
  mutate(
    # mean PPT at each site (all three trials required)
    primary_ppt   = if_else(PPTcompleteYN %in% c(1, 3),
                            (PPTindxR1Val + PPTindxR2Val + PPTindxR3Val) / 3, NA_real_),
    secondary_ppt = if_else(PPTcompleteYN %in% c(1, 2),
                            (PPTremoteR1Val + PPTremoteR2Val + PPTremoteR3Val) / 3, NA_real_)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # CPM compares remote PPT before conditioning with PPT during cold-water immersion
    ppt_cold      = (CPMPPTremR1Val + CPMPPTremR2Val + CPMPPTremR3Val) / 3,
    primary_cpm   = if_else(PPTcompleteYN %in% c(1, 2),
                            (secondary_ppt - ppt_cold) / secondary_ppt * 100, NA_real_),
    secondary_cpm = if_else(PPTcompleteYN %in% c(1, 2),
                            secondary_ppt - ppt_cold, NA_real_)
  ) |>
  select(-ppt_cold)
```

A look at the eight biomarker columns.

```{r}
#| label: peek

qst |>
  select(record_id,
         primary_ppt, secondary_ppt,
         primary_ts_index, secondary_ts_index,
         primary_ts_remote, secondary_ts_remote,
         primary_cpm, secondary_cpm) |>
  head()
```

Check that the biomarkers are stored as numbers.

```{r}
#| label: check-types

qst |>
  select(record_id, starts_with("primary_"), starts_with("secondary_")) |>
  glimpse()
```

### Data Quality

A few things are worth knowing before we start:

- **Biomarkers need complete trial data.** Each mean is computed only when all of its trials are present, so expect a modest number of missing biomarker values even among completed assessments.
- **CPM percent change can be extreme.** Dividing by the pre-immersion PPT means a small baseline can blow up the percentage, while the secondary CPM (a simple difference) stays bounded by the pressure scale. We tally the biomarker coverage first.

```{r}
#| label: qc-coverage

qst |>
  summarise(across(
    c(primary_ppt, primary_ts_index, primary_ts_remote, primary_cpm),
    \(x) sum(!is.na(x))
  ))
```

### Cross-Modality Links

Every file includes `record_id` and `subjectkey`, which uniquely identify a participant and let you link QST to other A2CPS modalities. QST is especially tied to imaging, since the cuff-pressure calibration used to evoke a target pain level in the scanner is shared between the two. To show the join running, we simulate a small table standing in for another modality: it carries the shared identifiers plus a made-up `cuff_pressure`. We set a seed so the simulated values are reproducible, and join on the shared identifiers, which `intersect()` finds automatically.

```{r}
#| label: cross-modality

# a simulated table standing in for another modality:
# every participant's identifiers plus a made-up cuff pressure
set.seed(1)
other_modality <- qst |>
  select(record_id, subjectkey) |>
  mutate(cuff_pressure = sample(20:60, n(), replace = TRUE))

inner_join(other_modality, qst, by = intersect(names(other_modality), names(qst)))
```

## Exploratory data analysis

The three assays are meant to capture different pain-processing mechanisms: static sensitivity (PPT), facilitation (MTS), and inhibition (CPM). We reshape the primary biomarkers into a long format and plot their distributions. Note the different scales: PPT and MTS are on a pressure or pain scale, while CPM percent change is unbounded and heavy-tailed.

```{r}
#| label: distributions

primary <- qst |>
  select(record_id,
         `PPT (index)`    = primary_ppt,
         `MTS (index)`    = primary_ts_index,
         `MTS (remote)`   = primary_ts_remote,
         `CPM (% change)` = primary_cpm)

primary |>
  pivot_longer(-record_id, names_to = "biomarker", values_to = "value") |>
  filter(!is.na(value)) |>
  ggplot(aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  facet_wrap(~biomarker, scales = "free") +
  labs(title = "Distributions of primary QST biomarkers (thoracic)", x = NULL, y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The CPM panel makes the heavy tail from the percent change easy to see. Next we look at how the biomarkers relate to one another using a spearman (rank-based) correlation on pairwise-complete observations.

```{r}
#| label: correlation

primary |>
  select(-record_id) |>
  cor(method = "spearman", use = "pairwise.complete.obs") |>
  round(2)
```

The pattern is informative. The two MTS sites are strongly correlated (around 0.75), so a participant who summates at the index site tends to also summate at the remote site. Otherwise PPT, MTS, and CPM are close to independent. The assays are **not** redundant: each biomarker adds its own information about a participant's pain-processing profile, which is exactly why A2CPS collects all three rather than a single summary of pain sensitivity.

## Considerations While Working on the Project

### Data Generation

QST is administered in person by trained study staff, following the A2CPS Manual of Procedures, which specifies the algometer and Neuropen procedures, the cold-water CPM protocol, and the index and remote testing locations. NDA stores the raw per-trial ratings, so the PPT, MTS, and CPM biomarkers are computed from those trials as shown above.

### Other

- **Directionality matters.** Higher PPT means less sensitivity, higher MTS means more facilitation, and negative CPM points to inhibition. A flipped sign quietly reverses a result, so the table above is a handy reference.
- **MTS and the wind-up ratio are non-negative by construction.** The difference and wind-up scores use `max(final, initial)` in place of the recorded maximum, so they never fall below 0 (difference) or 1 (wind-up ratio).
- **Extra assay.** The thoracic cohort also includes a Dynamic Mechanical Allodynia assessment, which is not part of the three biomarkers above but is available in the same file.
